evidence.reading: Six entity cross-reference rules exist in matched pairs, one per crate, and the predicates coincide: cobre-core `validate_line_refs` checks `line.source_bus_id`/`target_bus_id` against the bus registry, cobre-io `check_line_references` checks the same two fields against the same set. The filling rules coincide literally: `hydro.entry_stage_id.is_none()` under a present `filling`, and `filling.start_stage_id >= entry`, appear in both crates. `crates/cobre-io/src/pipeline.rs` is the only production `SystemBuilder::build` site in the workspace and it runs at :248, after `ctx.into_result()?` at :99 has already aborted on the cobre-io copy — so for every rule cobre-io duplicates, the cobre-core copy can only fire for a directly-constructed builder (tests and doctests), and a divergence between the two copies is invisible. The split ownership also shows in the error taxonomy: `LoadError::CrossReferenceError` (crates/cobre-io/src/error.rs:65) has zero production producers workspace-wide (the only non-test matches are two cobre-python consumers), because the referential layer routes its findings through `ValidationContext` into `ConstraintError` instead. Scope note: the cobre-core anchors belong to sub-station A; this candidate is filed on its cobre-io half.

candidates.fixShape: Name one owner per invariant class. The cross-reference and filling predicates are paradigm-neutral entity invariants, so either they live beside the entity in cobre-core and cobre-io's Layer 3 delegates to them, or cobre-io stays the sole owner and the cobre-core builder copies are deleted as unreachable — but not both, and the choice should be recorded once rather than settled per rule. Whichever direction is chosen, the diagnostic carrier has to follow it: today one side emits a structured ValidationError::InvalidReference and the other a formatted string, and cobre-io's own LoadError::CrossReferenceError variant is bypassed by its only would-be producer. If the consolidation moves rules down into cobre-core, keep the moved set strictly paradigm-neutral — a hydro-cascade or stage-horizon rule carried into L0 would trip the first conflicts trigger. Ancillary to the fix, not part of it: CrossReferenceError either gains the producer the consolidation implies or is retired with its two cobre-python match arms.

candidates.title: An out-of-horizon `stage_id` on a bound-override row is a hard error for two families and a silent drop for the other five

evidence.command: grep -rn 'not a valid study stage\|outside the study horizon' crates/cobre-io/src/validation --include='*.rs' | grep -v '///' && echo '--- 5a disclaims the stage axis ---' && sed -n '96,99p' crates/cobre-io/src/validation/semantic/block_bounds.rs && echo '--- the resolver drops the row ---' && grep -n 'let Some(&stage_idx) = stage_index.get(&row.stage_id) else {' -A2 crates/cobre-io/src/resolution/bounds.rs
evidence.reading: A stage-axis rule for bound-override rows exists for exactly two of the seven families: `thermal_bounds` (Layer 5a, `BusinessRuleViolation`) and `ncs_bounds` (Layer 3, `InvalidReference`). The block-axis rule in `block_bounds.rs` explicitly declines to own the stage axis in its own doc at :98-99. Downstream, `crates/cobre-io/src/resolution/bounds.rs` `continue`s past any row whose `stage_id` is absent from `stage_index`, at five stage-level sites and once inside `block_slot` at :675. So for `hydro_bounds`, `line_bounds`, `pumping_bounds`, `contract_bounds` and `hydro_unit_group_bounds` a row naming a stage outside the study is discarded with no diagnostic from any layer, while the identical mistake on a thermal or NCS row is a hard load failure. Scope note: resolution/bounds.rs is sub-station B's path and is cited as the downstream mechanism only; the missing rule is in sub-station C's validation modules.

candidates.fixShape: Give the stage axis the same table-driven treatment the block axis already has, so one rule covers every bound family instead of two families having bespoke rules and five having none. It belongs beside the block-axis rule in the Layer 5a family module, keyed off the same per-family descriptor and the same study-stage set, and it should reuse the crate's stage resolver rather than a fresh id-non-negative scan. Retire the thermal-only and NCS-only copies onto it so the classification stops depending on which family the deck touched. The resolver's tolerant skip stays as it is: it is correct precisely because the load has already been rejected before it runs.

candidates.title: The config admission rules are enforced only as a side effect of an accessor, and every cobre-io caller discards the resulting error on a premise the Layer-2 gate does not satisfy

evidence.command: grep -rn 'validate_scenario_source_cfg\|validate_openings_cfg' crates/ --include='*.rs' && echo '--- the whole Layer-2 config gate ---' && sed -n '159,177p' crates/cobre-io/src/config/mod.rs && echo '--- every cobre-io caller swallows it ---' && grep -rn -A3 'training_scenario_source(Path::new\|simulation_scenario_source(Path::new' crates/cobre-io/src --include='*.rs' | grep -E 'else \{|\.ok\(\)' && echo '--- the stated premise ---' && grep -rn 'Config is Layer-2-validated' crates/cobre-io/src --include='*.rs'
evidence.reading: Five config admission rules — historical-scheme restricted to the inflow class, seed required once any class leaves in-sample, `openings` only under `training`, historical year range ordered, `historical_years` only with a historical class — live in `validate_scenario_source_cfg` / `validate_openings_cfg`, whose only caller is `convert_scenario_source_config` at :227-228, itself reachable only from the two `Config::*_scenario_source` accessors. The Layer-2 gate `validate_config` checks exactly two other things and never resolves a scenario source, so the comment at scenarios.rs:459 asserting these reads cannot fail is not underwritten by anything. Every one of the nine cobre-io call sites discards the error with a let-else return or `.ok()`. The consequence is inverted enforcement: an invalid scenario-source config does not fail the load, it silently switches off the rules that read it — `check_external_scheme_has_files` returns before doing any work rather than reporting either the config defect or the missing external files. Rejection happens only later and elsewhere, at `crates/cobre-sddp/src/setup/mod.rs:385`, for callers that get that far.

candidates.fixShape: Move the admission decision to the point where the config is admitted, not to whoever happens to read it. Resolve both scenario sources once inside the Layer-2 config gate, report their failures into the validation context alongside every other layer's findings, and hand the already-resolved values to the semantic rules so those rules take a resolved value rather than a fallible accessor. The accessors then become infallible reads of an already-admitted config and the nine let-else arms disappear with the fallibility that motivated them. This is the 0a admission gate applied to the block that exists today: an unsupported combination becomes a rejection, never a silent ignore. Distinct from the registered three-representation item — nothing here is about Config versus the downstream params projections, only about where Config's own rules are enforced.

candidates.title: The input-file registry is four hand-maintained parallel lists joined by position, guarded only by a length assertion

evidence.command: grep -n 'zip(manifest_fields_mut' crates/cobre-io/src/validation/structural.rs && sed -n '395,398p' crates/cobre-io/src/validation/structural.rs && echo '--- the only guard ---' && sed -n '612,623p' crates/cobre-io/src/validation/structural.rs && echo '--- registry sizes ---' && grep -c 'FileEntry {' crates/cobre-io/src/validation/structural.rs && grep -c 'pub [a-z_]*: bool,' crates/cobre-io/src/validation/structural.rs
evidence.reading: One input file is spelled in four places that must agree by hand: its path string in `FILE_ENTRIES` (43 entries, plus the one `struct FileEntry` declaration the count of 44 includes), its `bool` field on `FileManifest` (43 fields), its slot in the fixed-length 43-element mutable-reference array, and its path string again plus its field on `ParsedData` in `validation/schema.rs`. `validate_structure` joins the first and third by position, and the code itself states the failure mode at :397: a divergence silently misassigns presence flags. The only test guarding the join asserts equal length, by its own comment, so swapping two same-arity entries — two optional files in the same directory, say — leaves the assertion green while `validate_schema` reads the wrong file's presence flag and parses or skips the wrong file.

candidates.fixShape: Collapse the parallel lists to one keyed registry so a file is declared once and looked up by name rather than by ordinal. The manifest becomes a lookup keyed on the registry's own entry identity instead of a 43-field struct plus a 43-slot array, which removes the positional join and the hand-kept field order along with it. If the flat struct is worth keeping for its named-field ergonomics, the length assertion has to be replaced by one that actually pins the pairing, so a reordering fails the test rather than silently misassigning. The registry is also the place where the schema-export list and the parsed-data bundle should be derived from rather than restated, since all three enumerate the same set. Beyond the immediate fragility, a v1/v2 case-format shim has to describe two file sets, and doubling a four-way hand-join is a poor starting position for it.

evidence.reading: The check-and-emit shape for a dangling reference — index the rows, test membership in an id set, push an `InvalidReference` entry whose message reads "<RowType>[i] references non-existent <Entity> <id> via field '<field>'" — is written out 48 times in one file, spread over 13 functions; the shape is fixed enough that the module header at :22-24 prints it as a literal message template. The same station already solved the same problem the other way: `block_bounds.rs` carries the per-family constants in a `FamilyMeta` table and passes them to two shared emit helpers, so its six families cost one loop each rather than one hand-written block each. The same asymmetry holds for the study-stage set: 20 copies of the raw non-negative-id predicate across 11 validation modules, while `StageIdResolver` in the same crate declares itself the owner of the study-stage ids and is constructed independently at four further validation sites. candidates.fixShape: Align the referential module to the pattern its sibling already proves rather than propagating the open-coded one. A descriptor carrying the row label, source file, target entity name and field name, plus one emit helper taking a descriptor and an id set, collapses the bulk of the 48 blocks and makes the message template a single definition instead of a header comment describing 48 copies. Separately, derive the study-stage set and its stage-to-block-count map once at the entry to the validation pipeline and pass them alongside the parsed data, so the rules read one definition of a study stage instead of restating the pre-study-negative-id convention in each module. Both are behaviour-preserving as long as the emitted message text and ordering are pinned first; the diagnostics are user-facing and several tests match on their wording.

evidence.reading: The only index of the numbered semantic rules is the doc table in `semantic/mod.rs`, and nothing links a table row to the function that implements it: rules live in twelve sibling modules, are wired through two hand-maintained dispatch lists, and are described in a third place. Row 26 shows the drift that costs: it claims a live rule validating `simulation.sampling_scheme.type`, but that field no longer exists on `SimulationConfig` and `deny_unknown_fields` rejects it at parse time, as the config test at :1433 pins; grepping the whole validation tree for the field returns only the table row itself. The table is otherwise actively curated — eight rows carry an explicit retirement marker — so row 26 is drift, not a convention for retired entries. `dimensional.rs` keeps a fourth, separately numbered table for its own seven rules, so the numbering namespace is per-module by accident rather than by design.

candidates.fixShape: Bind rule identity to code so the registry cannot drift silently. The cheapest version keeps the table but attaches each rule number to its implementing function as a doc anchor, so a removed rule leaves a dangling reference the doc build notices. A stronger version drops the hand-maintained dispatch lists in favour of one table of rule entries the dispatcher iterates, which makes the number, the function and the registry one declaration. Either way row 26 needs a decision now — reinstate the rule for whatever replaced the field, or mark it retired the way the other eight are — and the per-module numbering namespaces should be stated as such rather than left to be inferred.
